title: Complete scam
body:
I didn't even make it past the privacy agreement before deleting. The five requests were:

1) I agree to the proceeding of my personal health information to enable core features 

2) privacy statement ans terms of service

3) I allow Propel to collect anonymous usage data to help improve the app and experience

4) I agree that Properly may use my personal data (except health data) to send product or service offers over email

5) I agree that AppsFlyer and its integrated partners may use information like my email and technical identifiers (within privacy policy) to help Propel show relevant advertising and reach people like me

Edit after Developer response on 7/9/2026: "Individual options" was not my experience. App store reviews do not allow screenshots, but I have them of the agreements screen. Any ability to move forward was prevented even with partial selections of the 5 agreements, and no differentiation was made clear between necessary and "optional" choices.

title: I Love It!!
body:
This app is really great! Yes you have to pay for it beyond the 7 day free trial, but it’s worth some money. Pro tip: deny all of the payment plans, including the free trial (there IS a free version) until it offers the premium version for $35.99/year forever! That’s about $3/month — more than reasonable. 

As for the games, they’re simple enough to start and then progressively get more challenging as you prove you can handle it. I like how they are not overly complicated. It keeps me coming back. I’m happy to have something leisurely to do on my phone that doesn’t involve wrecking my dopamine system (i.e. scrolling social media). And better yet, it’s helping my ADHD brain. Also loving the minimalist, sleek design.

author: yoass.com

title: “Free” trial actually costs subscribers $10
body:
After downloading and playing this game for ~ 45 minutes, I came across several claims that caused me to question the integrity of the developers. 

1) upon opening the game, one of the first screens claims something to the effect of, “#1 downloaded ADHD app/game.” Given that Propel currently has <600 reviews and the App Store doesn’t indicate # of downloads, it seems safe to say that statement is misleading. (I understand that such statements have become more normalized, but that doesn’t make the en any less deceitful.)

2) After answering the demographic and “let’s create your plan” questions, I was faced with the option to sign up for a “3-day free trial” followed by a $49.99 annual subscription fee. I clicked “see other plans” and was surprised to find the annual plan offered for $39.99 “(no free trial)”. Charging subscribers that opt to use the trial $10 more than those that subscribe sans the trial does not equal “free”; rather, it equals $10/3 days, or $3.33/day.

3) Finally, I played almost every game at least twice.  I’m apparently quite good compared to all the other users because I scored better than 93-95% players on EVERY game I played…including the game that I quit four times (number sort with the moving tiles). Quitting the game resulted in a ZERO score every time, and I STILL scored higher than 93% AND 94% of other players! According to this game, I’m decently bright (it is the #1 downloaded ADHD game 😉) but I can’t figure out how I could improve my standing -within minutes! - with the lowest possible score.    Assuming that the lowest possible score is ZERO (were negative scores possible, I would have received one based on how many moves I made before quitting), it’s not statistically possible for someone who scores 0 (the lowest possible score) to have outperformed 93% of users, because no one can score worse than 0. 
This statistical & coding oversight led me to conclude that the ego-boosting performance stats at the end of games are in place only to keep players playing. Presenting users with a sense of achievement is valuable…especially to the developer. 

If the developer is truly interested in helping those with ADHD (or anyone), they need to attend to the studies that indicate that honest, direct feedback is far more beneficial than sugar-coated or insincere. Instead of spitting out false numbers, consider offering tips on how to improve their gameplay. You ask for and benefit from in-app feedback so you can improve your game; extend the same courtesy to your users.

title: Updated - NOW for colorblind
body:
Original review below, but just bumped right to 5 full stars. Developer reached out on colorblind options, made numerous changes beyond feedback. While I haven’t seen all the new changes, I can confirm several games work significantly better, and a toggle now exists without user profile for colorblind users. GREAT JOB DEV! Thank you for the adjustments. 

———

Onboarding literally asks if you are colorblind, and regardless of what you say you are repeatedly shown color based puzzles without any patterns/textures to assist those who cannot see colors. Could be matching games based on colors, or games where words are a color and you are supposed to know if the color matches the word. Just not a great showing to be aware enough this condition exists, to ask about it, and to do nothing within the app itself to support users suffering from it.
